title: The encircling prayer
hookLine: Celtic Christians drew a circle around themselves with a finger, praying for protection
last: YOUR LOVE AND GRACE ARE ENOUGH.

lines: A NEW STRETCH: THE CELTIC WAY.
cards: A finger, pointed out at arm's length. A person turns slowly in place, sunwise, tracing a circle in the air all the way around. Then they step forward, and tradition says the circle goes with them.
That's a picture from the Gaelic Christian world of the Scottish Highlands and islands, and it begins a new stretch of this year's path: the Celtic way of prayer.
Prayer close to the ground, to weather, to doors and roads and hearths. Today's word: caim. The encircling prayer.

teach.b: Caim is a Gaelic word, given in English as a circle or an encompassing. The prayers that go with it ask God to surround a person: before and behind, above and below, on the right hand and the left.
Some were said for oneself, some over a child, a traveler, a house.

teach.h: THE CIRCLE IS GOD, NOT A WALL.
teach.b: And notice what the circle is. It isn't a magic boundary. In the prayers, the circle is God.
The person isn't building a wall; they're naming what's already around them. The Psalms already have the same picture.
Psalm one hundred twenty-five: "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people." The hills around the city become a picture of God on every side.
Psalm one hundred thirty-nine says it more closely still: "Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me." Beset, hemmed in, but by care.
The caim has a cousin you met on day one thousand twenty-three: the old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, which tradition gives to Patrick.
One stretch of it names Christ with me, before me, behind me, in me, beneath me, above me. Same shape: a person at the center, and Christ named in every direction. Why a finger?

Because a gesture can carry a prayer when words won't come, in a hospital corridor, at a bus stop, beside a crib, without anyone hearing a word. And the prayers don't promise that nothing hard will happen.
They name who is in the circle when it does.

how: In the Gaelic tradition recorded in the Scottish Highlands and islands, a person in danger would trace a circle around themselves with a finger while praying for God's protection; some Christians today use caim prayers in personal and community prayer.

o: a Celtic charm drawn on doors to keep spirits out
a Gaelic prayer of God encircling a person on every side
a Gaelic word for the stone ring around a holy well

s: in the caim prayers, the circle is a magic wall
in the prayers the circle is God, named on every side, not a wall the person builds.
Psalm 125 pictures the LORD round about his people like mountains
"as the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people."
the caim promises nothing hard will happen
the prayers name who is in the circle when hard things come; they don't promise they won't.

games.q: you're about to walk into a hard conversation, and you remember the old Gaelic prayer. what does the caim do?
o: trace a circle and name God around you.
build a wall to keep everyone out.
games.why: the caim names God on every side. it's a gesture you can make anywhere, without anyone hearing a word.

practice: If there's room, stretch out your right hand, one finger pointing, and turn slowly, or just sweep your arm around you, tracing a circle; then rest your hand in your lap.

Name what's inside the circle with you: someone you love, a worry, the room itself. If you pray, say the psalm's line, thou hast beset me behind and before; if not, just sit inside the shape you drew.

wordCard.voice: Caim. A Gaelic word for an encircling: a gesture and a prayer that name God on every side of a person.

carryVoice: Your line: circled by god. The circle goes with you when you step forward. Same time tomorrow.
